column2: Dab rubbing alcohol on one arm and water on the other. The alcohol feels colder and dries much faster. A vapor monitor reads far higher over the alcohol. What are the alcohol molecules doing, compared with water molecules, that lets them escape into vapor so easily?
column3: Alcohol molecules have weaker intermolecular attractions than water, so a larger fraction of particles can overcome cohesive forces at room temperature to evaporate.
column4: Intermolecular force strength dictating relative vapor pressure and volatility

column2: You pull some warm water into a plastic syringe. You cap the tip so no air can get in. Then you pull the plunger back hard. The water starts to boil in your hand. You did not heat it. What are the water molecules doing that lets the water boil without heat?
column3: Water molecules at the surface keep escaping into vapor. At this temperature they have a set vapor pressure. Pulling the plunger lowers the external pressure on the water. When that external pressure falls to the water's vapor pressure, molecules inside the liquid can escape into bubbles of vapor, so the water boils. The molecules already have enough energy; no heat is added.
column4: Boiling happens when the external pressure on a liquid falls to its vapor pressure; vapor pressure depends on temperature

column2: A toy bird sits beside a cup of water. You wet the felt on its head. Soon it tips forward, dips its beak in the water, and swings back up. It does this again and again. It has no battery and no spring. What are the molecules doing, on the wet head and inside the sealed glass, that keeps the bird moving?
column3: Water molecules on the wet felt evaporate; the most energetic ones leave cooling the head. Inside the sealed glass, the cooler head has a lower vapor pressure than the warm body: vapor condenses on the cold glass, and fewer molecules escape from the cold liquid. The higher vapor pressure in the warm body pushes liquid up the neck. The top grows heavy and the bird tips.
column4: Vapor pressure depends on temperature; a temperature difference inside a sealed container makes a pressure difference that can move liquid

column2: Far down on the sea floor, very hot water pours out of a rock chimney. A probe in the stream reads hotter than a pizza oven. Yet no steam bubbles form. At vents in shallower water, the hot water fizzes. What are the water molecules doing that keeps the deep water from boiling?
column3: Water molecules in the hot stream move fast, and many have enough energy to escape into vapor. But a bubble can only form if the vapor inside it pushes back as hard as the water pressing on it. Deep down, the weight of the water above squeezes the molecules together and keeps them from spreading apart into vapor. That pressure is very large, so the water must be much hotter before its vapor pressure is high enough to open a bubble. In shallower water the pressure is lower, so the water reaches its boiling point at a lower temperature, and it fizzes.
column4: Boiling happens when the vapor pressure reaches the pressure on the liquid; more pressure means a higher boiling point
